Chapter 3: The Struggle with Instability, Addiction, and Broken Promises
You know, in a lot of working-class families, that dream of stability—having a safe place to land—always seems just out of reach.
For this boy, life felt like a constant shuffle. New schools. New homes. New faces coming and going. Every move sparked fresh hope that things would finally get better... but more often than not, those hopes just turned into another letdown.
His mom’s struggle with addiction hovered over everything like a heavy cloud. Some days, she’d be filled with energy, making big plans and talking about the future.
Other days, she’d be lost in pain or quick to anger, and the boy learned to stay on his toes—always scanning for clues about what kind of day it would be.
He became an expert at reading the subtle signs. Maybe it was a sharpness in her voice, or a certain look in her eyes. He knew those signals meant trouble was coming, and he braced himself.
The adults around him tried to pitch in, but honestly, they were fighting their own battles too. Relationships were fragile, trust could vanish in a heartbeat, and promises... well, those were made and forgotten all the time.
The boy figured out pretty quickly that he couldn’t really count on anyone for long.
And it wasn’t just his family. Addiction was everywhere—neighbors, friends, other relatives.
Why? Sometimes it was pain. Sometimes just boredom, or that creeping sense of hopelessness. But the result was always the same: families breaking apart, jobs lost, and kids left to figure things out on their own.
Thankfully, his grandparents tried to be his safe haven. Their house was the one place he could relax—even if just for a little while.
Mamaw, with her sharp tongue and fierce kind of love, always made the rules clear. No excuses. She expected him to do his best, no matter what was happening back home.
Papaw was quieter, but you could count on his steady support.
Their presence gave him a sense of security he just couldn’t find anywhere else.
Still, even at their house, the old scars lingered.
Sometimes a simple argument would explode into something physical. Other nights, he’d hide in his room, listening to adults fighting just down the hall.
He learned how to cope by keeping his feelings locked up and pretending everything was fine—even when it was far from it.
Most people don’t really see the toll instability takes on kids.
They miss how it shapes who you become, or how it makes trusting others feel impossible.
For a lot of kids, the only way to survive is to toughen up—to slip on this mask of indifference so no one sees how much it hurts.
As the boy got older, he started to notice the patterns that kept his family stuck.
He saw how addiction and instability seemed to feed each other, forming this cycle that felt impossible to break.
And it was so easy to just give up, to believe that nothing was ever going to change.
But here’s what’s important—there were still moments of hope.
Small victories, like a good grade at school, a kind word from a teacher, or a peaceful evening at home, gave him a glimpse of what life could be.
It became clear: getting out of that cycle wasn’t about luck. It was going to take determination, real support, and the guts to imagine something different.
